stage_before: Charge phones and power banks, and fill containers with clean water.
Move documents, medicine and food to a high place, and pack the items listed above.
Agree a meeting point and route with your family.
Download this area's map to your phone, and switch off the electricity if water may enter the house.
stage_during: Leave early: do not wait for the water to reach the house, and follow local authorities.
Never walk, swim or drive through moving floodwater: it hides holes, wires and debris.
Stay away from electric wires and anything wet that is plugged in.
If you are trapped, go to the highest dry place and send the help SMS; keep the family together.
stage_after: Return only when officials allow it; avoid damaged buildings and floodwater.
Boil or treat all drinking water, and throw away food that touched floodwater.
Watch for diarrhoea, fever and skin infections; use ORS and seek care early.
Watch for snakes and other animals sheltering in dry places.

nisar_sub: NASA-ISRO L-band radar, two polarizations (HH and HV)
nisar_open_sub: NASA-ISRO L-band vs Sentinel-1, HH vs HV
nisar_intro: NISAR is the new NASA-ISRO radar satellite (L-band, about 24 cm wavelength). Radar sees through cloud, day and night. Smooth water reflects the signal away, so water looks dark. NISAR data is public from 17 June 2026, so this shows the 2026 monsoon.
nisar_swipe: Move the line to compare the two sides
nisar_s1_line: Sentinel-1 ({d}, {g} days apart): about {km} km² of water
nisar_confirm: NISAR {pol} also sees {p}% of Sentinel-1's water as water.
nisar_unclassified: {pol}: the Otsu rule found no clear threshold on this date, so no water map was made (nothing guessed).
nisar_no_s1: No Sentinel-1 image within 3 days, so no comparison.
nisar_why_title: Why does NISAR see more water?
nisar_why: L-band's longer wave passes between rice seedlings or grass and reaches the water below. Sentinel-1's C-band (about 6 cm) stops more at the plants. So paddies flooded for transplanting look like water to NISAR, often not to Sentinel-1. SafeWindow looks for flooded roads, and paddy water rarely blocks roads, so for its main result Sentinel-1's behaviour is the useful one.
nisar_groups_title: What the radar signal looks like (this date, median values)
nisar_group_row: HH {hh} dB · HV {hv} dB · HH−HV {d} dB
nisar_groups_note: Lower dB means darker in the radar. This only describes the signal; no new class is made from it.
nisar_pol: Polarization is the direction the radar wave vibrates when sent and received. HH: sent and received horizontal; smooth water looks very dark, so water is easy to find. HV: sent horizontal, received vertical; messy things like vegetation send more of it back, so plants look bright. Together they help tell open water from vegetation.
nisar_rgb_legend: In the colour composite: red = HH, green = HV, blue = HH−HV. Black or dark blue = open water; greenish = vegetation; bright red-pink = buildings or very strong reflections.
nisar_limits: There is no independent field map, so this is agreement between radars and polarizations, not ground validation. Dates up to 16 October use NASA's provisional NISAR product; from 21 October the validated product (V1). Water areas from the two products, or from different orbit tracks, are not directly comparable. Water uses the same rule as Sentinel-1 (Otsu); nothing was tuned for NISAR or HV. Within 4 km of a NISAR frame's edge the signal fades and looks dark like water, so that strip is left out.
nisar_none: No NISAR layers have been made yet.
nisar_hv_text: At Trimmu on 18 June and 12 July, HH showed no clear threshold between water and dry land, so by the rule no HH water map was made. HV did show one on the same days, so HV gave a map. When one polarization fails, the other can still help. On days when both work, the HH and HV water maps largely agree (71–93%).
bld_what: Buildings drawn from satellite images by Google Open Buildings ({n}). Each building gets the same rule as a village: can it reach a shelter over open roads, and is mapped water within 50 m.
bld_far: More than 500 m from a road (boat-dependent): {n}
bld_priority_title: Where to check in the field first
bld_priority_how: How: each cell's score = the buildings seen isolated, added up over the radar dates. More buildings isolated on more dates come first. It says where to look first; it is not a rescue list.
bld_cluster: {km} km from {v} ({m} m cell): {b} mapped buildings; up to {i} isolated at once; on {n} radar dates; first {d}
bld_none_isolated: No mapped building was seen isolated.
bld_limits: Remember: a mapped building does not mean people are there. Near water does not mean water inside; radar often misses water between buildings, and haor homes stand on raised ground. Google's building list has errors too (only buildings with confidence above 75% are used). Shelters are not verified.
legend_buildings: Mapped buildings ({m} m cells; bigger circle = more buildings): red = some isolated, yellow = uncertain, green = connected, grey = far from roads; blue ring = within 50 m of water
bld_tip: {n} mapped buildings · isolated {i} · uncertain {u} · near water {w} · far from roads {f}

nisar_series_note: Square kilometres of water in the study area on each NISAR date, for NISAR HH, NISAR HV and the nearest Sentinel-1 pass. A missing point means that radar found no clear water threshold that day: nothing was guessed.
nisar_series_alt: Line chart of water area in square kilometres on each NISAR date. The numbers are listed below it.
nisar_gap_title: Water only NISAR sees, around each village
nisar_gap_head: On this date, within 3 km of {n} of {total} villages, NISAR sees at least 10 percentage points more water than Sentinel-1 (median gap {m} points).
nisar_gap_none: No comparison for this date: it needs a NISAR water map and a Sentinel-1 one.
nisar_gap_note: A large gap most likely means water under plants (rice paddies flooded for transplanting, flooded grass), which L-band reaches and C-band does not. This measures the gap; it cannot say which cause it is, and there is no field data. It is not a flood warning.
